endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Document how the problem/solution justifies the use of AI

endorsements.title: Developing, purchasing, implementing and monitoring AI tools in radiology: practical considerations. A multi-society statement
endorsements.issuer: ACR, CAR, ESR, RANZCR, RSNA; Radiol Artif Intell 2024 (PMID 38251899, doi:10.1148/ryai.230513)
endorsements.quote: In either case, as outlined in Section 4A, it is essential to determine whether or not the tool solves a real, specific problem that the institution has; tools are solutions, and a solution to a non-existent problem has no value.

endorsements.title: Key decision points in adopting an AI solution
endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership (Duke Health and partners)
endorsements.quote: Also includes guides for determining different dimensions of problems and assessing the suitability of AI as a technical approach to address problems.

endorsements.title: Health Equity Across the AI Lifecycle (HEAAL) framework
endorsements.issuer: Health AI Partnership; PLOS Digital Health (PMID 38723025, doi:10.1371/journal.pdig.0000390)
endorsements.quote: It involves defining the intended and unintended use, constraints, and the target population for the solution.

endorsements.title: Action Guide: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
endorsements.issuer: National Association of Community Health Centers
endorsements.quote: The HEAAL Framework focuses on five assessment domains: accountability, fairness, fitness for purpose, reliability and validity, and transparency. These domains are aligned with the Eight Key Decision Points in AI adoption and include procedures that should be applied across each stage.

endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Who specifically are the intended users (e.g., physicians, registered nurses, medical students, call-center agents, patients), and do the users have appropriate licensure, expertise, and availability?

endorsements.title: Machine learning for healthcare that matters: Reorienting from technical novelty to equitable impact
endorsements.quote: Engage with clinical stakeholders early in the clinical process, and working from problem to solution with earnest evaluation of whether a particular method—or machine learning at all—is most appropriate to address the problem.

endorsements.title: Practical Applications of Large Language Models for Health Care Professionals and Scientists
endorsements.quote: In summary, to address the various challenges arising from the use of LLMs, we believe that a multistage evaluation process is indicated: first, it should be determined which tasks can be appropriately outsourced to such a tool and weighed up against potential implementation hurdles [ 17 , 18 ].

endorsements.title: An Evidence-Based Framework for Patient-Facing Artificial Intelligence Integration in the Emergency Department
endorsements.issuer: Journal of the American College of Emergency Physicians open
endorsements.quote: The key question is not whether artificial intelligence is available, but whether it adds measurable value over existing workflows for specific ED populations and tasks.

endorsements.title: Human-centered digital ecosystem: safeguarding healthcare workers' sleep, ergonomics, and occupational health
endorsements.quote: Before introducing AI, healthcare organizations should first determine whether unnecessary work can be eliminated, whether workflows can be simplified, and whether interoperability or conventional automation can reduce duplicate data entry.

endorsements.title: A Responsible AI Readiness Framework for Digital Self-Management Platforms: Illustrative Application to a Rule-Based GERD Platform
endorsements.quote: Gate 0 therefore asks whether AI offers meaningful incremental value over explicit rules and whether representative data, valid labels, human oversight, lifecycle monitoring, and proportionate resources are available.

evidence.title: Occam’s Razor in AI-assisted complex diagnosis: a comparative effectiveness study of single large language models versus multi-agent systems in resource-constrained primary care settings
evidence.outcome: Accuracy, safety, and latency of complex multi-agent systems versus simpler single model
evidence.effect: Single GPT-oss-20b outperformed multi-agent ensembles; safety score 5.50 vs 4.99 (p<0.001); Top-1 accuracy 51.58% vs 46.89%; latency 30s vs 200s (85% reduction).
evidence.quote: Furthermore, the inclusion of mid-tier models in the adaptive workflow introduced an "ensemble degradation" effect, significantly lowering the Safety Score compared to the single GPT-oss-20b model (4.99 vs 5.50; p < 0.001) and reducing the rate of Top-1 correct diagnoses from 51.58% to 46.89%.

evidence.title: Assessing the Limitations of Large Language Models in Clinical Practice Guideline-Concordant Treatment Decision-Making on Real-World Data: Retrospective Study
evidence.outcome: Whether a simple non-LLM model matches LLM performance on treatment decision
evidence.effect: Simple reference model performed comparably to GPT-4 and outperformed LLMs on raw reports, suggesting simpler models could suffice.
evidence.quote: In our study, as well as in the study by Salihu et al [ 8 ], simple reference models performed comparably to GPT-4, suggesting that non-LLM models could outperform LLMs if trained appropriately.

evidence.title: Bigger Is Not Always Better: Computational Efficiency in Lexical Prehospital Triage Modeling
evidence.outcome: Whether complex transformer models outperform simpler models and at what computational cost
evidence.effect: Transformers gave no meaningful performance gain (AUROC .803 vs .793). Training took 7:14 (BioBERT) and 3:57 (DistilBERT) vs 9.42 s for MLM. Prediction took 13.36 s and 7.37 s vs .048 s.
evidence.quote: Our findings counter the "bigger is better" paradigm in medical AI: MLMs performed equivalently to LLMs in task mirroring on-scene triage while requiring a fraction of the computational resources.

evidence.title: Evaluating the Diagnostic Classification Ability of Multimodal Large Language Models: Insights from the Osteoarthritis Initiative
evidence.outcome: Classification accuracy of full MLLM pipelines versus a trained vision encoder alone for knee OA
evidence.effect: A trained vision encoder alone outperformed full MLLM pipelines in classification accuracy. Fine-tuning the LLM gave no meaningful improvement over prompt-based guidance.
evidence.quote: In our classification task, a trained vision encoder alone could outperform full MLLM pipelines in classification accuracy and fine-tuning the LLM provided no meaningful improvement over prompt-based guidance.

evidence.title: LLM is Not All You Need: A Systematic Evaluation of ML vs. Foundation Models for text and image based Medical Classification
evidence.outcome: Performance of classical ML versus prompt-based and fine-tuned foundation models on medical classification
evidence.effect: Classical ML (LR, LightGBM, ResNet-50) achieved best overall performance across most tasks; Gemini 2.5 zero-shot performed poorly on text tasks, and LoRA-tuned Gemma performed worst across all experiments.
evidence.quote: According to our results, traditional machine learning (ML) models set a high standard by consistently achieving the best overall performance across most medical categorization tasks.

evidence.title: 40 years of actigraphy in sleep medicine and current state of the art algorithms
evidence.outcome: Whether complex AI outperforms simpler methods on sleep scoring
evidence.effect: Complex ML/DL models did not outperform simple regression/heuristic algorithms; simpler methods were slightly superior and complex models seemed to generalize poorly.
evidence.quote: The performance of complex machine learning and deep learning models seem to suffer from poor generalization.

evidence.title: Summary Report of the SNMMI AI Task Force Radiomics Challenge 2024
evidence.venue: Journal of nuclear medicine : official publication, Society of Nuclear Medicine
evidence.outcome: Whether complex radiomics ML models outperform simple regression models on the same prediction task
evidence.effect: Some models showed better FOMs than simple linear or logistic regression using SUV and TMTV, but differences were nonsignificant, indicating limited or no added value from complexity.
evidence.quote: This suggests that, for the challenge dataset, there was limited or no value seen from the addition of sophisticated radiomic features and use of machine learning when developing models for outcome prediction.
evidence.sample_unit: submitted models (19 continuous-outcome, 12 binary-outcome) from challenge teams

evidence.title: A comparative performance analysis of regular expressions and a large language model-based approach to extract the BI-RADS score from radiological reports
evidence.outcome: Whether LLM outperforms simpler non-AI method for structured extraction task
evidence.effect: LLM was no more accurate than Regex (87.69% vs 89.20%, P = .56) and far slower (1687.20 s vs 0.06 s).
evidence.quote: Compared to the LLM-based method, Regex processing was more efficient, completing the task 28 120 times faster (0.06 seconds vs 1687.20 seconds).

evidence.title: Evaluation of Large Language Models as Emergency Department Revisit Predictors
evidence.venue: Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing. Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing
evidence.outcome: Whether complex LLM approaches outperform simpler non-LLM model for the task
evidence.effect: Simple LightGBM on structured EHR features (F1=0.4614) exceeded all LLM-based methods (F1=0.3022-0.4505).
evidence.quote: However, we also found that a structured EHR baseline achieved performance (F1=0.4614 (95% CI [0.4496, 0.4789])) that exceeded LLM-based methods (F1=0.3022–0.4505).

commentary.bottom_line: One benchmark of 915 complex clinical cases found a single model outperformed multi-agent ensembles on safety, accuracy, and latency, and eight hazard studies found simpler or non-AI methods matched or exceeded complex AI across several tasks. No study tests whether documenting AI justification or reassessing model-task fit before deployment changes outcomes in real deployments.

perspectives.view: The only test of the practice, a patient-free benchmark, compares two AI designs rather than a documented justification process. Certainty is very low because the evidence is indirect, comes from one study, and has no clinical setting. The eight hazard studies agree that complexity often adds little, which supports the premise but does not test the safeguard.

The single model scored 5.50 on safety versus 4.99 for multi-agent ensembles (p<0.001). Complex sleep-scoring models seemed to generalize poorly compared with simple heuristics. These results suggest added complexity may bring failure modes without accuracy gains. No study shows that a pre-deployment fit review catches such problems before they reach patients.

An LLM took 1687.20 s versus 0.06 s for Regex at similar accuracy (87.69% vs 89.20%, P = .56). Multi-agent latency was 200 s versus 30 s for a single model. LightGBM on structured EHR features (F1=0.4614) exceeded all LLM methods across 138010 ED visits. A fit review would likely need to run comparisons of this kind.

Transformer training took 7:14 (BioBERT) and 3:57 (DistilBERT) versus 9.42 s for a simple model, with AUROC .803 versus .793. Classical ML led on most tasks in one benchmark. A vision encoder alone beat full MLLM pipelines for knee OA. Radiomics models showed nonsignificant gains over regression. A documented comparison may avoid spending on complexity that adds little.

Only one hazard study, 80 patients from Germany tagged as a non-English population, involved language diversity. In that study a simple reference model performed comparably to GPT-4. The single test of the practice used benchmark cases from China and reported no Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy representation.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployments that underwent a documented AI justification and model-task fit review with deployments that did not. Such a study would measure accuracy, safety events, cost, and later de-adoption. Prospective or stepped-wedge evaluations embedded in health-system AI governance, including safety-net sites, would address this gap.
commentary.underserved_note: The one test of the practice did not report Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Among the hazard studies, only pmid:41190890 involved non-English data. The evidence therefore cannot show whether fit reviews work in settings that serve these populations.
